Bring the whole family for a day of cultural discovery, live performances, hands-on activities, and opportunities to connect with the people and traditions that help make Louisiana so unique. Celebrate the rich heritage and living cultures of Indigenous and Afro-Indigenous communities through traditional and fancy dancing, storytelling, music, poetry, cooking demonstrations, films, and more! Throughout the village, meet tribal members, artists, and cultural representatives as they share their stories, languages, traditions, and crafts. Explore cultural displays, watch demonstrations, visit artisan tables, and participate in hands-on activities for children and families. More than a celebration of history, Indigenous Peoples' Culture Day highlights the vibrant cultures, creativity, and traditions that continue to thrive today and the lasting contributions of Indigenous and Afro-Indigenous communities to Louisiana's cultural heritage. Since it highlights the hunting heritage of the Acadiana region, the Duck Festival offers the public great entertainment with its Duck and Goose Calling Contest, Skate Shooting, Dog Trials, Duck Dash, and Decoy Carving. item.name: Abbeville's Giant Omelette Celebration
item.description: In 1984, three members of the Chamber of Commerce (Emery "Bichon" Toups, Tracy Kays, and Sheri Meaux) attended the Easter Omelette Festival in Bessieres, France and were later knighted the first of Abbeville's Chevaliers. They returned home with the determination to bring Abbeville closer to its French Heritage by hosting an omelette festival and joining the sisterhood of cities who celebrate the omelette - Bessieres, France; Frejus, France; Dumbea, New Caledonia; Granby, Quebec in Canada.; Malmedy, Belgium and Pigue, Argentina later joined the fraternity, bringing the number making seven locations to celebrate this festival annually. Abbeville's Giant Omelette is truly an international festival. Each year, foreign representatives from each of these cities arrive here to be knighted as chevaliers (chefs) into Abbeville's Confrerie (fraternity). On Concord Street, which stretches from the majestic moss-covered live oak trees in historic Magadalen Square to the live oaks in front of the Vermilion Parish Courthouse, they help to prepare the 5000 egg Giant Cajun Omelette. They also come to experience the area's joie de vivre, to share its rich culture, to meet and mingle with its people, and to make memories and friendships which last a lifetime. The omelette is then given away freely to all in attendance. Come join in our Celebration and become closer to our French heritage through the cooking of the "Omelette of Friendship". This unique Celebration is unique to Louisiana in the United States

Top of the Teche benefits the work of the Arnaudville Chamber of Commerce and the Leonville Volunteer Fire Department. Paddling Bayou Teche is made possible by the efforts of the non-profit organization, TECHE Project. The TECHE Project began as a small, volunteer clean-up organization. Today, the group is responsible for the bayou’s designation as a National Paddle Trail by the U.S. Park Service and a National Water Trail by the U.S. Interior Department. The team has also added trailheads and floating docks to communities along the Teche featuring a water-proof map for canoers marking attractions, restaurants, and historic sites along the trail. item.name: Original Southwest Louisiana Zydeco Music Festival
item.description: The 45th Original Southwest Louisiana Zydeco Festival is live! Organizers are preparing to satisfy the demand for Creole Culture and Zydeco Music. Festival executive director Lena Charles says that locally and nationwide, music fans are eager to return to Southwest Louisiana to experience firsthand the original flavor of Zydeco and Creole Culture. The festival takes place on September 4, at the Yambilee Festival Grounds with multiple activities leading up to that date. In the 1970s, The Treasures of Opelousas, a group of concerned citizens, feared that Zydeco (La La) Music and Creole Culture was dying out; they responded and organized the first festival in 1982, “Unbroken.” Forty-four years later, we are still celebrating and promoting the best of creole culture, traditional food and of course, The Best of Zydeco Music. Zydeco Season begins with a pre-party on August 6, and ends with a day jam-packed full of Zydeco celebrations on Sept. 5. Learn more at www.zydeco.org or on Facebook at SWLA Zydeco Music Festival. FESTIVAL EVENTS THURSDAY AUGUST 6, 2026: PRE-PARTY Join us for a pre-party for 44th Annual - Media Day-at the Opelousas Museum with refreshments, music and celebration of the 2026 Zydeco Season. The event takes place from 12 noon to 1:30 p.m. at the Opelousas Museum, 315 N Main St, Opelousas, LA 70570. SATURDAY, SEPT 5, 2026: THE ORIGINAL SOUTHWEST ZYDECO FESTIVAL The Festival takes place on the Yambilee Festival Grounds at 1939 W. Landry St. Opelousas, LA 70570. The event runs from 12 noon until the wee hours of the night. Gather friends and family and plan your reunions for a full day and night of music, traditional Creole food by vendors and food trucks, and arts and crafts. Bring your lawn chairs and plan to stay for all events, “I promise you will have a BON TON.” Learn more at www, zydeco.org or Facebook swlazydecofestival. Come Celebrate 44 Years of Culture & Zydeco! “Pa Kase`,” Le`ritage de Zariko

item.name: Fête-Dieu du Teche
item.description: The 9th annual Bayou Teche Eucharistic Procession will head South for a one-time Bayou Extravaganza! Families and parishes are encouraged to register a boat or gather at one or more of the stops along the procession route. The day begins at 8 am with the Mass of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary in French by Bishop Douglas Deshotel at the Church of the Assumption in Franklin. Following the Mass there will be a procession with the Blessed Sacrament to the nearby boat landing. At 9:30 am boats will depart in the procession up Bayou Teche toward New Iberia. Residents living along the route are encouraged to gather and greet the Blessed Sacrament as it passes near their home. The boat procession will stop at boat landings in the towns along the Teche for Rosary and Benediction (arriving in Baldwin at 11:00 am, Charenton at 12:30 pm, Jeanerette at 2:30 pm and finally the park in New Iberia at about 4:45 pm). Upon arriving in New Iberia, a foot procession will commence to St. Peter Catholic Church for Solemn Vespers at 5:30 pm and Final Benediction at 6:00 pm. Confession will be heard in mobile units at each of the stops along the way. Pope Francis has granted participants of Fete Dieu du Teche a Plenary Indulgence, valid on August 15th for those who attend the 8 am French Mass in Franklin, or make the procession by boat, or those who participate in the devotions at one of the many stops along the Teche. Those who are impeded for a serious reason from physically attending the procession may also gain the indulgence by spiritually uniting their prayers and trials. The Holy Father asks participants to pray for fidelity to the Christian vocation, for the good of the family, and for priestly and religious vocations. If you don't have access to a boat, follow by vehicle and join us at one or all of the stops for the Rosary and Benediction. For more information, email us at fetedieuduteche@gmail.com or call 337.394.6550.

item.name: Eunice Mardi Gras Celebration
item.description: This five-day celebration is not your typical idea of Mardi Gras. There are no beads and doubloons here. Instead, in Eunice, Louisiana, men and women on horseback don hand-crafted wire masks, tall hats called capuchons , and colorful costumes. The main event is the Courir de Mardi Gras & Chicken Run. Here, revelers chase a chicken or guineafowl and participate in Medieval begging practices. The courir takes place on Mardi Gras day and is only one part of the celebration. Starting the Friday before Mardi Gras Day, you can cut loose all weekend long. Dance in the street at music concerts and jam sessions. There are even activities for children and teenagers at the Lil’ Mardi Gras held on Sunday. Also on Sunday is an old-time boucherie (hog butchering). The Eunice Courir de Mardi Gras dates back to when the town was first established in the late 19th century. The courir was abandoned for a few years during World War II, but in 1946 a small band of riders revived the tradition. Today, the Eunice Courir de Mardi Gras has more than 2,000 participants on the run. It continues to increase each year.

item.name: Curtis Patterson — Persistent Vision, Sculptures from 2011 – 2026
item.description: A Shreveport native returns to Louisiana with fifteen years of bronze and steel sculpture drawn from African diasporic motifs and the rhythms of jazz. September 19, 2026 – February 20, 2027 Curtis Patterson works with what was handed to him. Rhythms from jazz. Symbols carried across the Atlantic and kept alive for generations. He does not quote these traditions. He extends them and keeps them moving. Patterson came of age in Louisiana during the civil rights era, and that experience continues to inform his sculpture. He was born in Shreveport in 1944 and has lived and worked in Atlanta most of his life. In the studio, jazz gives him his method: he sets a structure in bronze or steel, then bends and tests it until instinct carries it somewhere new, a freedom abstraction allows. The forms, released from resemblance, become visual metaphors steeped in history and cross-cultural exchange. Persistent Vision brings together more than fifteen years of work. The Rocker series, begun in 2011, balances motion and stillness in interlocking forms. Diasporic Reflections (2021) presents mask-inspired wall reliefs exploring transformation and personal expression. Shango’s Friends (2025–26) draws on Yoruba symbols such as the double axe and double iron. item.name: Elemore Morgan Jr. — Photographs from the Festival of American Folklife, 1976
item.description: Presented by Festivals Acadiens et Créoles in collaboration with the Smithsonian Folklife Festival and Center for Louisiana Studies Printed from the original slides and exhibited for the first time, paired with ephemera from the artist’s papers, twenty-three photographs are presented fifty years on, during America’s 250th Anniversary. October 9, 2026 – December 19, 2026 In the summer of 1976, the Smithsonian’s Festival of American Folklife ran for twelve weeks on the National Mall as the centerpiece of the nation’s Bicentennial, the country’s 200th birthday. A collective of Cajun and Creole musicians from South Louisiana took to the stages as recognized bearers of a national heritage. Louisiana artist Elemore Morgan Jr. (1931-2008) traveled to the Festival in Washington, D.C. with his camera, drawn by a question larger than the event itself: what is America, and who are the people who make it? Known for his landscape paintings, Morgan engaged the world constantly through his lens, and at the Festival he turned it on the performers from home and the crowds who gathered to hear them. Among them were ballad singers Inez Catalon, Lula Landry and Alma Barthélémy, the Balfa Brothers with Ally Young, the Ardoin Family with Canray Fontenot, Nathan Abshire, Vinesse Lejeune, Lionel Leleux, Don Montoucet, and Elton Quibodeaux, playing alongside Native American, Haitian, Québécois, and French musicians. Morgan moved beyond the stages into the demonstration areas, markets, and monuments, where artisans and craftspeople worked at their trades. In all of it, he found his own region held within a wider American story, distinct and shared at once. Morgan gathered these images for his AMERICA SERIES, an ambitious body of painting he imagined but never fully realized, and the Festival gave him its vocabulary. “I must return [to painting],” he wrote in his diary on July 6, 1976, “and above all, attempt to realize some of these American ‘ideas’ as paintings. By sharing my slides frequently and getting to know these images, I believe I am stocking up my memory or imagination with my own special vocabulary of forms, which, I hope and trust, will come out as uncontained composites, poetic images based on the experience of [being] in this part of the planet.” Morgan wasn’t only documenting other artists at work. Through the camera, he was taking in the country and its people, building the vocabulary his paintings would draw upon. That purpose gives these images their charge. Morgan’s eye for gesture, light, and texture frames performers, audiences, and the exchange between them with sensitivity, drawing the viewer closer to the ties between people, place, and tradition. By turning his lens on the crowds as often as the performers, he caught the country celebrating its own culture. They are at once witness and interpretation, document and authored image: a nation reflecting on itself. Here, the line between record and artistic vision blurs. The exhibition asks how photographs like these shape a shared understanding of a historical moment while leaving room for evolving and individual truths. Elemore Morgan Jr. — Photographs from the Festival of American Folklife presents 23 photographs printed from Morgan’s original slides and exhibited for the first time, alongside ephemera from the artist’s archives, shown fifty years on, during America’s 250th. Together they return to the questions that originally drew Morgan to the Mall: what makes a people, and what holds their differences together? This project received funding from the Smithsonian’s “Our Shared Future: 250,” a Smithsonian-wide initiative supported by private philanthropy and created to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary and advance the Smithsonian vision for the next 250 years.

item.description: Come out to Vermilionville, the cultural arm of Bayou Vermilion District, to experience a traditional Mardi Gras run Sunday, February 23, 2025. The whole family can participate in this interactive event where the Basile Mardi Gras Association shares in the medieval tradition of the Courir de Mardi Gras. Disguised revelers, led by Le Capitaine and singing La Chanson de Mardi Gras will make their way through the historic village begging for the ingredients to make a gumbo. The event will begin at 10 a.m. with a screening of Pat Mire’s iconic Mardi Gras documentary, “Dance for a Chicken,” which reveals the secrets and history of the rural Mardi Gras run or Courir. At 11 AM, musician Kevin Rees will demonstrate the use of the “Chanson de Mardi Gras,” with the attendees. At 11:30 AM, the Basile Mardi Gras Association will begin the run through the historic village and will end with the famous chicken chase for children. After the run, grab a delicious lunch at Vermilionville’s restaurant, La Cuisine de Maman, then join us in the dancehall for live music from the Pine Leaf Boys, 1 PM – 4 PM. There will be king cake tasting and a Capuchon (traditional pointy hat) craft for the kids as well! This is one historic event you will not want to miss. Mark your calendars and come pass a good time with us at Vermilionville this Mardi Gras season

item.name: Matthew Day Jackson — Yesterday’s Tomorrow
item.description: Presented by the Emory Family Jackson’s paintings, sculptures, and designs transform the gallery into a domestic space that explores how close we’ve come to a future earlier generations imagined. September 19, 2026 – August 2, 2027 A steel frame stands open in the gallery, outlining three rooms of a home. Brooklyn-based artist Matthew Day Jackson built everything inside them: paintings, furniture, and sculpture made from Formica, laminate, and molded plywood, joined by ceramics from Laura Seymour, his partner. These are the materials that filled American kitchens after World War II, sold as clean, modern, and made to last. A home dressed in them was a piece of tomorrow a family could own. Jackson takes that promise as his subject and its surfaces as his medium. Jackson works across painting, sculpture, furniture design, photography, video, and installation, and every painting here is built rather than brushed. He traces an image by hand, cuts its shapes from Formica, and fills them with oil paint and poured lead, so a countertop laminate becomes the picture itself. His furniture travels the opposite way, taken apart from mid-century originals and rebuilt as designs of his own. The confidence that put Formica on the counter also put a man on the Moon. Jackson recreates the images of that era’s ambition, LIFE magazine, the Apollo landing, the American frontier, in the materials of the home, so the ambition that reached the Moon shares a room with the ambition that bought a new kitchen. Yesterday’s Tomorrow holds that promise, now more than half a century old, in the present tense. Its objects, built from a future first pictured in postwar America, stand in one open frame where time runs in both directions. Together they measure how close we came to the future earlier generations imagined, and how much of it we are still building. Yesterday’s Tomorrow is presented by the Emory Family with major support from the Hilliard Exhibition Fund.

item.name: Tour du Teche 135
item.description: Tour du Teche 135 is an annual race for canoes, kayaks, pirogues (the traditional Cajun canoe), and SUP’s along the entire length of Bayou Teche in southwestern Louisiana, a total of 135 miles (217 kilometers) including small sections of Bayou Courtableau and the Atchafalaya River. It’s a three-day staged race beginning the first Friday in October. There are two classes of Tour du Teche 135: Pro Race, in which some of the fastest boats and paddlers from around the world vie for cash prizes; and Voyageur Race (or recreational). Pro class winners have their names placed on the race monument in Berwick at the Finish area. Tour du Teche 135 was begun in 2010 with the dual purpose of introducing the beautiful Teche Country to paddlers and other eco-tourists from beyond and to illustrate for its residents the recreational, aesthetic, cultural, and economic value of Bayou Teche. Since the race’s inception, these two groups, visitors and locals, have met and mingled in happy expositions of music and cuisine that give Tour du Teche 135 its reputation as a moveable party as well as a tough series of paddle marathons.

item.name: A Century in Focus — Images from Women Photographers of the 20th Century
item.description: Explore the groundbreaking work of twenty women photographers whose images redefined visual storytelling and shaped the field of photography. September 19, 2026 – February 20, 2027 Photography changed the way we see and remember the world. Throughout the twentieth century, women photographers pushed the medium beyond documentation, using it to explore identity, place, beauty, struggle, and everyday life. In times of profound social and political change, the photographers in this show each found their own ways to make sense of a rapidly changing world. Some turned their cameras toward the realities around them. Dorothea Lange and Sabine Weiss used photography to illuminate the effects of economic hardship, migration, and changing cities. Others, including Anne W. Brigman and Ruth Bernhard, embraced experimentation, abstraction, and artistic expression, demonstrating how photography could be as imaginative and expressive as any other art form. Together, their work challenged traditional ideas about what photography could be—and helped establish it as one of the defining artistic and cultural languages of the twentieth century. Working across documentary photography, photojournalism, portraiture, abstraction, and experimentation, these artists created images that continue to shape how we understand modern life. Their photographs offer intimate glimpses of people and places while inviting us to consider larger questions of family, memory, resilience, and social change. At a time when photography—and the worlds it recorded—were changing quickly, these women claimed space for their own perspectives and ways of seeing. Their contributions challenged the narratives of art and journalism and opened doors for generations of women photographers and image makers to follow. The photographs in this exhibition remind us that photography is more than a record of what happened. It can be a way of looking closely, asking questions, finding connection, and making the unseen visible. Many of these images were made decades ago, yet their human stories and questions continue to resonate today. Featuring works by Linda Alterwitz, Ruth Bernhard, Ilse Bing, Margaret Bourke-White, Anne W. Brigman, Debbie Fleming Caffery, Anna Eaton Collins, Adrian Deckbar, Abbey Drucker, Antoinette Marie Ducrest, Mildred Grossman, Dorothea Lange, Helen Levitt, Rose Mandel, Allison Petit, Barbara Riley, Sandra Russell-Clark, and Sabine Weiss. This exhibition is supported by Janine and Craig Thomson and the Robert and Jolie Shelton Exhibition Fund, with generous contributions from Jeanine Piskurich.

item.name: Speaker Series: An Introduction to Atakapa-Ishak Language and Culture
item.description: Join us for a presentation on the Atakapa-Ishak Language and Culture by Dr. Jeffery U. Darensbourg on Saturday, December 5, 2026 at 1 p.m. The event will take place at the Opelousas Museum at 315 N. Main Street, Opelousas, LA 70570. Dr. Darensbourg will explore the language and culture of the Atakapa-Ishak. The Ishak are an Indigenous people who have lived in southwest Louisiana and southeast Texas since precolonial times. Various organized groups of Ishak exist currently, and while federal agencies have documented the Ishak in the past, no current Ishak groups enjoy federal recognition. Many Louisiana Creoles have Ishak ancestry, causing the group to be known sometimes as “Creole Indians.” The tribe has had a lasting influence on zydeco music, and its language is undergoing a resurgence. Jeffery U. Darensbourg is a Louisiana Creole and member of the Atakapa-Ishak Nation. Louisiana’s deep histories of ethnic mixing between European, African, and Indigenous Peoples are reflected in both his ancestry and work. He works with words, crafting essays, poetry, academic articles, and public talks intertwining traditional academic research with autoethnography and memoir. Darensbourg has an M.L.I.S. from Louisiana State University, and a Ph.D. in Cognitive Science from the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. Dr. Darensbourg’s presentation is a part of a speaker series titled, Opelousas, Up Close and Personal. The Speaker series is funded by the Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities’ 2026 Rebirth Grant and will cover topics pertaining to topics in Opelousas’ rich history. Other presentations in the series cover topics such as the Louisiana Civil Rights trail, the Yambilee and Yamba Celebrations, the Civil War, and local participation in the Civil Rights movement. Funding for the 2026 Rebirth Grant has been provided by the State of Louisiana and administered by the Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities. item.name: Blown Away on the Bayou - A Harmonica/Blues Summit
item.description: Blown Away on the Bayou Sunset, Louisiana The idea for Blown Away on the Bayou came about through a series of pie and tea conversations with founders Jim Phillips, Christy Leichty, and Grant Dermody. A shared love of music led to the idea of a harmonica summit to celebrate and teach the rich history of the harmonica in Acadiana, touching on both Blues and Cajun styles. In 2021 the inaugural Blown Away on the Bayou took place at the Whirley Bird, an underground honky-tonk located in Sunset, Louisiana. Year two saw the expansion to include Blues guitar, mandolin, fiddle, accordion, and the addition of vocal instruction. As the Summit continues to grow, the founders intend to provide an immersive experience where Blues lovers from all over the U.S. and abroad can learn, share, play, dance, and eat together. The mission of Blown Away on the Bayou is to enrich cultural understanding, nurture musical passion, and celebrate the Blues in the Acadiana region. Participants, both in our region and well beyond, are offered an immersive experience to explore the profound impact of the Blues, to dig more deeply into the study of Acoustic Blues, and to come to an understanding of its historic significance. The Summit offers a space to experience, discuss, demonstrate and jam the blues openly, thereby creating an environment that will encourage those in attendance to discover their own unique approach to the Blues and to play with their own authentic voice. Join us for the third annual Blown Away on the Bayou Harmonica/Blues Summit in the heart of Acadiana. World-class musicians and teachers from Louisiana and beyond offering beginning, intermediate, and advanced Blues instruction in harmonica, guitar, mandolin, fiddle, and accordion. Full-time, part-time, drop-in, seminars available. Don’t play, or don’t want to take lessons? No problem! We have live music and dancing too!

item.description: The International Rice Festival held annually in Crowley is one of Louisiana's largest and also it's oldest Agricultural Festival. Since it's first festival on October 5th, 1937, over 7 million people have attended the annual event. The celebration brings attention to the importance of rice as food and also emphasizes it's place in the world's economic picture. It is usually held on Friday and Saturday of the 3rd weekend in October. Location is Downtown Crowley. There are 2 parades, Friday (Children's Day), which is the Children's Parade, and Saturday, the Grand Parade. There are also Special Events including the Rice Cooking Contest, Rice Eating Contest, Farmers Banquet and also the Queens Ball. There is also entertainment continuously from early morning to midnight. Also in conjunction with the Festival, is an Arts and Crafts exhibit, which is held adjacent to the Festival Grounds and also on Main Street. For more information click here.

item.name: Creole LaLa
item.description: FREE family-friendly community gathering that blends language, music, food, and culture. The event begins with a Creole French lesson; designed for beginners but welcoming to all levels. Afterward, the space transforms into an open music jam, where musicians of all ages and skill levels- sometimes including Grammy-nominated artists- sit in the circle together. It is not uncommon to see children playing alongside seasoned musicians, creating an atmosphere that is both educational and inspiring. To further foster fellowship, we serve a free meal and invite local small businesses to set up and share their work with the community. This not only strengthens cultural connections but also supports the local economy. This event fills a vital gap in our community. Before we began in July of 2024, there was no monthly space dedicated specifically to celebrating and practicing Creole French while also engaging in music and cultural exchange. Now, we consistently welcome over 100 people from diverse ages, backgrounds, and even countries, coming together in a safe, inclusive environment. The result is something truly special- a place where people can learn, connect, and celebrate Louisiana Creole culture in a way that is vibrant, welcoming, and sustainable.

item.name: Sebastian Lodrige: Burden | Artificial & Natural
item.description: I am unnaturally attracted to the easily accessible universe that is media and entertainment. Movies, Video games, and social media have become vices I’ve accepted within my daily life. This consumption has been present within my life for as long as I remember. As a kid I used to go outside enjoying my wild nature running through the woods and playing in the mud but whenever I got my first video game console the world outside seemed less enticing. I had multiple worlds at my fingertips, these worlds begging to be explored. What started as an experience of adventure and joy became an escape from the world I lived in. It seemed easier to escape into a character rather than face the world that asked who you are. In video games I could be whoever, through movies I could project myself onto the actors portraying my favorite characters. I thought as I grew up this was natural, this is how I was and that’s okay. Though these past times quickly went from escape to obsession. I realized I was isolating myself from reality, locking myself in my room for hours to experience these artificial worlds not embracing the real one I’m currently living within. Only now a 22-year-old do I realize how dishonest I have been with myself and I feel on the precipice of great change. I want to reconnect with the world that has been unnatural to me for so long, this heavy burden that is outside my comfort zone and which makes me utterly uneasy. Through my work I want to display the burden I feel in the natural world and artificial reality. The heavy toll it takes to enter this otherworld of the natural and the easily accessible artificial distractions I immerse myself in. This lightly grasped false happiness that I often subject myself to daily. This push and pull has been at the forefront of my life this past year and I wish through this art that I may either find a balance or a door to be present within my life and not let it pass me by.

item.name: Artists’ Alliance
item.description: Drawing heavily on the archives of the late artist group, the Artists’ Alliance, AcA will mount a retrospective that showcases the work of this influential group of artists and reimagine what is was like to be there in person. Visitors will experience their past performances through multiple gatherings during the run of the show as well as a relaunch of their signature event Tattooed Walls. This exhibition will allow us to introduce a new generation of audiences to a very important group of artists who set the stage for our contemporary art landscape, this being done right next door in the old Lafayette Hardware Store. This building cradled their creativity and allowed these artists to create challenging and experimental works as well as a home for communal gatherings. In telling the story of these artists, we will also be sharing an important chapter in the history of this significant landmark in our community. item.description: Spend some time with voices from the past at the St. Landry Catholic Church Cemetery Tours & Historical Reenactments in the Zydeco Capital of the World, Opelousas. This historical group tour will transport you back in time. Reactors focus on a chosen time period in Opelousas’ history and are dressed the part. You’ve heard of New Orleans’s famous haunted tours, but you’ve never seen a tour done by the ghosts themselves. Tour the cemetery where Napoleonic General Garrigues de Flaugeac and Louisiana Governor Jacques Dupré are interred with your ghostly guides. All proceeds from the cemetery tours fund the Cemetery Historical Restoration Project. The tours began in 2003 and, to date, 30 plus gravesites have been restored. Saturday tours take place at 6pm, 6:30pm, 7pm, 7:30pm, and 8pm, while Sunday tours are at 2pm and 3pm. Handicapped accessible tours will be available. Call the organizer for more details. item.name: Holy Ghost Creole Festival
item.description: Experience Creole culture at the Holy Ghost Creole Festival in Opelousas, Louisiana. Every year, the festival kicks off with Friday morning finger-lickin’ fried catfish. That night, experience gospel hymns featuring several choir groups from Holy Ghost Catholic Church. Saturday, the festival grounds open early with live music and more Creole food to sample including their famous backbone stew and barbeque pork steak. Dinner tickets may be purchased at the Church Parish Office until the day of the event, or you may purchase tickets on the grounds. That morning, participate in the 5k run or 1-mile fun walk to prepare for a day of amazing food. Pies, boudin, cracklins, and other great local foods will be sold each day of the festival. All-day long, hear zydeco music bands under the music tent, but be sure to take a break to seek out the festival’s famous sweet dough pies. Holy Ghost volunteers spend hours preparing and baking this local treat because they are just too tempting to pass up. Sunday, join the locals in celebrating their Creole heritage at the Creole Festival Parade. The route runs from Landry Street all the way to Union Street. Feel free to bring lawn chairs or a blanket to enjoy the parade. The festival takes place every year, on the first weekend in November.

item.name: Blackpot Camp
item.description: Even as an adult you can still have a good time at camp! At Black Pot Camp, work with professional, award-winning musicians from across the U.S. These artists include your favorite Creole and Cajun music artists, including The Revelers and artists who will be performing at the Annual Black Pot Music Festival, which kicks off on the last day of camp. Activities for campers include Cajun fiddle, accordion, guitar, songwriting, and so much more. Participants will also try their hand at Cajun cooking, taught by locals in a hands-on working environment. It’s not all workshops at Black Pot Camp. Every night, campers take a break from lessons for a music concert in the barn turned dancehall. Overall, the camp has a loose, festive atmosphere that encourages extracurricular jamming and sharing of experiences among campers from all places and backgrounds. If you’ve never tried to Cajun waltz or square dance, now is the time to take your cue from experienced instructors. All of the activities are in the spirit of fun! Create unforgettable memories with interactive experiences among other lovers of Cajun and roots music. Black Pot Camp takes place the last week of October on the beautiful, secluded grounds of Lakeview Park & Beach, located in Eunice, Louisiana. There’s plenty of space for an RV in addition to cabins and room for tent camping. Admission for this event varies. You can learn more at BlackPotCamp.com. Be sure to also look into their volunteer program. P.S. – You don’t need to be a camper to attend dances in the barn. There’s a general admission so anyone can join the fun! Dances take place in the evening. Contact Lakeview Park & Beach for evening event details.
